You are RhD negative, the minus in a blood group like A- (or II-): your red cells carry no RhD protein, usually because the RHD gene is missing from both of your chromosomes. About 15 in 100 people in Europe are RhD negative, far fewer in East Asia. Antibodies against RhD appear only after meeting RhD-positive blood, for example in pregnancy with an RhD-positive baby, and they could affect a later baby. That is why RhD-negative mothers are offered a protective injection; the decision always uses the mother's lab blood group, never a DNA file. If you are planning a pregnancy, your doctor or midwife can test your RhD status.
